name: XBOW
summary: XBOW builds autonomous offensive-security software designed to find and validate vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.
overview: XBOW is an AI-powered penetration-testing company that helps security teams identify exploitable weaknesses. It announced a $120 million Series C in March 2026, led by DFJ Growth and Northzone, at a valuation above $1 billion.

facts.label: Latest financing
facts.note: XBOW announced a $120 million Series C that valued the company at more than $1 billion.

bull_case: Autonomous offensive testing can address a persistent security-talent bottleneck if XBOW turns high-quality findings into a trusted enterprise workflow.
bear_case: False positives, responsible-use requirements, and intense security-platform competition can limit deployment and pricing power.
latest_round: March 2026: $120M Series C at a reported $1B+ valuation
directory_notes: Public financing and operating data remain limited.

intelligence.description: AI-powered offensive security and autonomous penetration testing for enterprise defenders.
company: XBOW develops an autonomous hacker intended to surface exploitable vulnerabilities before they are used in live attacks. The company sells offensive-security capabilities to defenders seeking more continuous testing than conventional manual penetration testing can provide.

In March 2026, XBOW announced a $120 million Series C led by DFJ Growth and Northzone at a valuation above $1 billion. The financing included Sofina, Alkeon Capital, Altimeter, NFDG Ventures, and Sequoia Capital.
intelligence.why_it_matters: Security is one of the clearest enterprise markets for applied AI because the cost of finding threats early is measurable. XBOW is a prominent private bet on automating offensive testing without handing control to attackers.

changed.text: XBOW announced a $120M Series C at a valuation above $1B.

takeaways: The March 2026 Series C established a valuation above $1B.
Enterprise trust and actionable findings are the central adoption variables.
Responsible use and category competition remain material risks.
